a:T738,The method, AdaBPE, keeps the overall BPE-style vocabulary induction setup but changes the merge selection criterion. Instead of using a fixed minimum frequency or a pure pair-frequency greedy rule, it introduces an adaptive frequency threshold that depends on two variables.

First, token length. Longer candidate patterns are allowed to survive at lower raw frequency if they provide larger compression benefit. This is meant to correct a known bias of standard BPE-like procedures: they repeatedly absorb frequent short fragments even when those fragments are not the best units for reducing encoded length.

Second, pattern type. AdaBPE explicitly distinguishes general-language patterns from formal-language patterns, with special attention to LaTeX. Different threshold schedules are applied to these categories, so low-resource symbolic structures can still enter the shared vocabulary even when they are globally less frequent. In effect, this is a lightweight capacity-allocation mechanism during vocabulary learning, without resorting to separate vocabularies.

The paper frames this as adaptive frequent-pattern mining followed by BPE-based vocabulary construction. That distinction matters. The novelty is not merely allowing merges across whitespace, which SuperBPE-like methods already do. The novelty is deciding which cross-boundary patterns deserve vocabulary slots, using criteria tied to compression and sublanguage imbalance. This should make the tokenizer more likely to capture multiword expressions and structured LaTeX units rather than only frequent short spans.

An engineering detail worth noting is the choice to stay close to the BPE family instead of moving to a globally optimized but expensive segmentation procedure. The paper is aiming for a practical tokenizer upgrade that can fit existing pretraining pipelines.b:T6a3,The evaluation has two layers.

First, tokenizer-level analysis. Across five datasets covering both general language and LaTeX-heavy or structured content, the paper compares AdaBPE against standard BPE and SuperBPE along encoding efficiency, supertoken contribution, and token-distribution statistics. The main result is consistent: AdaBPE improves compression on domain-specific symbolic content while avoiding degradation on general language. That domain split is the key result. A tokenizer that helps LaTeX but hurts ordinary text would be hard to justify for general pretraining; the paper argues AdaBPE avoids that trade-off.

Second, small-scale LM training. The authors train small language models with AdaBPE and SuperBPE tokenizers and evaluate them on five downstream benchmarks. The gains are reported mainly on tasks involving structured notation, mathematical expressions, or mixed text-symbolic inputs, while general-language performance remains comparable. This matches the intended mechanism: better tokenization should shorten sequences and preserve meaningful symbolic units, which in turn should make modeling easier.

From a pretraining perspective, the most important ablations are the ones isolating the two adaptive components: length-aware thresholding alone, type-aware thresholding alone, and both together. Those ablations determine whether the method works mainly because it captures longer units, because it protects LaTeX-like patterns, or because the two effects are complementary. The abstract does not expose the exact numbers, so the full paper should be read with attention to compression deltas, average sequence-length reduction, and absolute downstream gains.c:T52c,This is a skim paper, but it is worth reading selectively if tokenizer design matters to your work.

Start with the problem setup in the introduction, especially the two failure modes labeled around length insensitivity and underrepresented formal languages. That framing is the strongest part of the paper.

Then read the method section carefully enough to understand the adaptive threshold formula. The practical questions are: how the threshold scales with token length, how pattern types are identified, and whether the LaTeX/general-language distinction depends on rules, annotations, or simple heuristics. That determines how portable the method is to code, HTML, Markdown, or other symbolic sublanguages.

Next, focus on the tokenizer analysis rather than only the downstream table. Compression, token-length distribution, and the composition of learned supertokens will tell you whether the gains come from a genuinely better vocabulary or from training noise.

Finally, inspect the task mix in the LM experiments. If the improvements are concentrated on math or LaTeX-related tasks while general language stays flat, that is already a meaningful result.

Estimated reading time: 25–35 minutes. If time is tight, read the motivation, the method figure, the token statistics tables, and the main downstream results.d:T4e9,On-Policy Self-Training has four main stages. First, from a topic descriptor, the model synthesizes a question and privileged information, typically including an answer or reasoning context. No human-written problem or reference solution is used. Second, the generated samples are filtered. Pseudo-verification checks whether the problem is well formed by asking the model to reproduce the answer in a fresh context and under paraphrasing. A consensus gate checks whether the problem is still useful for the current student: if the student already reproduces the answer consistently across on-policy rollouts, the sample is discarded. This makes the curriculum move as the student improves. Third, training uses on-policy self-distillation. The student sees only the question, while the teacher sees the question plus the synthetic privileged information and provides dense next-token targets at states visited by the student. This asymmetry matters: SFT or RL would optimize directly against the synthetic answer, while OPST uses that answer as context that lets the teacher generate a richer reasoning trajectory from its parametric knowledge. Fourth, the loop is repeated across rounds, with an EMA teacher used to reduce self-induced distribution drift.e:Tc55,模型是 decoder-only causal Transformer，但关键在若干组合设计。

一是混合注意力。Kolibri 在 50 层中采用 4:1 的 SWA 与 full attention 交替：每 5 层里 1 层 full attention，其他 4 层用 512 token 窗口的 sliding-window attention。这样做的目的很明确：大部分层用局部注意力压低训练和解码成本，少量 full attention 层负责全局信息混合。更有意思的是位置编码并非统一处理。SWA 层使用 RoPE，full-attention 层则使用 NoPE；同时对 Q、K 做 per-head RMSNorm，且在 SWA 层中先 norm 再加 RoPE。这个组合反映出作者的判断：局部窗口层需要显式相对位置信号来稳定局部建模，而全局层若继续叠加 RoPE，可能在长上下文外推或注意力尺度上带来额外负担，NoPE 反而更干净。论文把这些不是当作独立 trick，而是作为 hybrid attention 的配套设计来选。

二是 MoE 稀疏结构。每层有 384 个 routed experts，每个 token 选 6 个 routed experts，再加 1 个 shared expert；router 用 sigmoid logits，但 top-k 后不再归一化。这一设计明显受 DeepSeek 系 MoE 影响，目标是让路由权重表达更灵活，同时通过 shared expert 提供稳定的通用通道。负载均衡使用 EQB 和 LEI，而不是传统单一 auxiliary loss。Kolibri Origin 则是另一套更简单、稀疏度更低的对照架构：8-of-128 routed experts，前两层 dense，全层 full attention。作者通过代理实验逐步走向更高总容量、更低 active ratio 的 Kolibri 主架构。

三是 tokenizer。词表大小 128k，采用 UniBPE。它仍是自底向上的 merge 过程，但每一步 merge 选择依据是 Unigram loss，而不是标准 BPE 的频次启发式。作者特别强调德语形态学边界：与 GPT-5 tokenizer 相比，Kolibri tokenizer 在德语上有 65.2% 的 token 边界落在 morpheme boundary，而对方是 47.3%；在德语网页文本上 token 数减少 11.2%。这不是小修小补，因为德语复合词和屈折变化多，tokenizer 若切分不合理，会直接影响 token budget、上下文利用率和训练信号密度。

四是训练流程。Kolibri 总训练量 24T tokens，包含 pre-training、mid-training 和 long-context extension；目标最大上下文训练到 256k。作者没有只做一次大规模训练，而是先在 M/L 两个代理尺度上做受控消融。M 规模是 7.8B total / 0.6B active，训练 97.6B tokens；L 规模是 30.6B total / 2.1B active，训练 327.6B tokens。模型形状 sweep 时，还会在最小代理尺度上调学习率，而不是完全相信 scaling-law 预测值，避免把 shape 优劣和 learning-rate 失配混在一起。这一点很专业，也很少在公开报告里讲得这么明确。

五是效率与部署导向。Kolibri 的设计目标不是单纯追求 benchmark 峰值，而是追求 Pareto frontier：在给定 active compute 下尽量提高质量，同时保持开放权重、可控数据链路和适合受监管场景的部署属性。因此很多选择都偏向“可解释、可复现、可部署”，而不是最激进的实验性结构。f:Ta18,最重要的数字先列出来：Kolibri 主模型 78.1B 总参数，3.46B active parameters per token，活跃比例 4.4%；50 层；48 个 query heads、4 个 KV heads、head dim 128；MoE 为 384 experts 中选 6 个 routed experts 加 1 个 shared expert；训练最大上下文 256k；总训练量 24T tokens，其中 pre-training 20T，long-context 阶段 200B。Kolibri Origin 为 30.6B total、3.27B active、64k context，是更早期的对照版本。

论文实验的价值主要在消融，而不是单个榜单名次。首先是 tokenizer 结果：德语上 morpheme boundary 对齐率 65.2%，对比 GPT-5 tokenizer 的 47.3%；德语网页文本 token 数减少 11.2%。这说明 UniBPE 的收益不是抽象的“更适合多语”，而是直接体现在德语 token 效率上。

其次是架构代理实验。作者在 M/L 两个代理尺度上比较 full attention 与 hybrid attention、不同窗口大小、位置编码方案、QK norm、MoE 稀疏度、路由与负载均衡策略。虽然给出的全文片段没有展开所有表格数字，但从方法描述可以看出，作者评估每个改动都看三件事：建模质量、attention/MoE 稳定性、训练与解码效率。这个评价框架比只看 validation loss 更完整，因为很多 MoE 或长上下文设计在 loss 上看不差，但会在负载、溢出、解码延迟上出问题。

再者，Kolibri 与 Kolibri Origin 的对比本身就是一个重要实验结论。两者 active 参数接近，分别是 3.46B 和 3.27B，但总容量从 30.6B 提升到 78.1B，同时 active ratio 从 10.7% 降到 4.4%。这意味着作者在近似相同每 token 计算下，换来了更大的总模型容量和更长上下文能力。若最终质量也同步提升，那么这就是很典型的 Pareto 改进。

长上下文方面，Kolibri 把训练上下文扩到 256k，而不是停在 64k。论文提到部分消融会在 pretrain 后直接接一个缩短版 long-context phase，用来快速比较不同设计对长上下文能力的影响。这种做法很实用，因为完整长上下文训练成本很高，先用短版 extension 做架构筛选能节省大量预算。

如果精读全文，建议重点找以下具体结果：1）hybrid attention 相对 full attention 的 loss/benchmark/吞吐变化；2）NoPE 只放在 full-attention 层是否优于全层 RoPE；3）6-of-384 与 8-of-128 在相近 active compute 下的质量差异；4）EQB+LEI 相比传统 auxiliary balancing loss 的负载均衡曲线；5）mid-training 和 long-context extension 各自带来的增益幅度。10:T527,This is a high-value technical report for pretraining researchers because it exposes many recipe decisions with controlled proxy-scale ablations. Four aspects stand out.

First, it provides a rare large-scale bilingual recipe with German accounting for more than 20% of the data, and it ties tokenizer behavior to language efficiency instead of only reporting final benchmark scores.

Second, it presents a compute-conscious MoE design: 78.1B total parameters with only 3.46B active per token, or 4.4% active ratio. That makes the distinction between total capacity and per-token compute explicit.

Third, its attention design is not a default full-attention stack. It uses a 4:1 mix of sliding-window attention and full attention, together with a coordinated choice of RoPE, NoPE, and QK normalization. That is directly relevant to long-context pretraining, where component interactions often matter more than any single trick.

Fourth, it treats pretraining, mid-training, and long-context extension as one training continuum, totaling 24T tokens. That interface matters because many model capabilities are now shaped by later phases, not just by the initial pretraining run.

The contribution is best read as a strong recipe document: systematic, engineering-heavy, and useful as a reference for future model builds.11:Tca2,Kolibri is a decoder-only causal Transformer, but the interesting part is the combination of design choices.

The first is hybrid attention. Across 50 layers, the model uses a 4:1 ratio of sliding-window attention (SWA) to full attention: one full-attention block every five layers, with the other four using a 512-token backward window. The rationale is clear: most layers use local attention to reduce training and decoding cost, while periodic full-attention layers provide global mixing. Positional encoding is also split by layer type. SWA blocks use RoPE, while full-attention blocks use NoPE. In addition, queries and keys are normalized per head with RMSNorm, and in SWA blocks this happens before applying RoPE. This suggests a deliberate view: local-window layers benefit from explicit relative position structure, while global layers may be cleaner and more stable without RoPE, especially for long-context behavior.

The second is the MoE design. Each MoE layer contains 384 routed experts; each token is sent to 6 routed experts plus 1 shared expert. Router scores are sigmoids of router logits and are not renormalized after top-k selection. This is clearly influenced by recent DeepSeek-style MoE choices. The shared expert provides a stable common pathway, while the sparse routed experts expand total capacity. Load balancing uses EQB and LEI rather than a single classic auxiliary loss. The earlier Kolibri Origin architecture serves as a contrast point: 8-of-128 routing, two leading dense layers, and full attention everywhere. The final Kolibri moves toward higher total capacity and lower active ratio at similar active compute.

The third is the tokenizer. The model uses a 128k-vocabulary UniBPE tokenizer. It still builds merges bottom-up like BPE, but chooses each merge using a Unigram-loss criterion rather than a pure frequency heuristic. The report emphasizes German morphology: compared with the GPT-5 tokenizer, 65.2% of token boundaries align with morpheme boundaries in German, versus 47.3% for GPT-5, and the tokenizer uses 11.2% fewer tokens on German web text. That matters because German compounds and inflection make tokenization quality directly relevant to token budget and training signal density.

The fourth is the training pipeline. Kolibri is trained on 24T tokens across pretraining, mid-training, and long-context extension, with a target context length of 256k. The team does not rely on a single expensive run. Instead, it performs controlled ablations on two proxy scales: M with 7.8B total / 0.6B active parameters trained on 97.6B tokens, and L with 30.6B total / 2.1B active parameters trained on 327.6B tokens. For shape sweeps, they also retune learning rates at the smallest scale rather than blindly trusting scaling-law predictions. That is an important methodological detail because architecture comparisons are often confounded by suboptimal learning-rate transfer.

The fifth is the deployment-oriented objective. The design target is a Pareto-efficient open model for practical deployment, not simply the highest possible benchmark score. That explains why many choices favor interpretability, reproducibility, and serving efficiency over more experimental architectures.12:T9dc,The headline numbers are straightforward: Kolibri has 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active parameters per token, a 4.4% active ratio. It has 50 layers, 48 query heads, 4 KV heads, head dimension 128, and a 6-of-384 plus shared-expert MoE pattern. It is trained up to 256k context and uses 24T tokens in total, including 20T pretraining tokens and 200B long-context tokens. Kolibri Origin is a 30.6B-total, 3.27B-active, 64k-context predecessor used as a reference point.

The most informative results are the ablations rather than a single leaderboard position. On tokenization, the report gives concrete evidence: 65.2% morpheme-boundary alignment in German versus 47.3% for the GPT-5 tokenizer, and 11.2% fewer tokens on German web text. That is a direct efficiency gain, not a vague multilingual claim.

On architecture, the proxy-scale studies compare full attention against hybrid attention, different window sizes, positional-encoding choices, QK normalization, MoE sparsity levels, and routing/load-balancing strategies. Even from the available text, the evaluation framework is clear: every change is judged on modeling quality, attention/MoE stability, and both training and decoding efficiency. That is the right lens for MoE and long-context design, where a method can look fine on validation loss but fail on load balance, overflow, or serving cost.

The comparison between Kolibri and Kolibri Origin is itself an important result. Active compute is similar, 3.46B versus 3.27B active parameters per token, but total capacity increases from 30.6B to 78.1B while the active ratio drops from 10.7% to 4.4%. If quality improves accordingly, that is a clean Pareto improvement: more total capacity and longer context at roughly similar per-token compute.

For long context, Kolibri extends training to 256k rather than stopping at 64k. The report notes that some ablations use a shortened long-context phase immediately after pretraining to compare design choices more cheaply. That is a practical and useful methodology because full long-context extension is expensive.

The deeper questions are whether the German-oriented tokenizer design transfers to other morphologically rich languages, whether the NoPE+RoPE layer split scales to larger long-context models, and when increasing total capacity at nearly fixed active compute starts to show diminishing returns.14:T848,The method has two conceptual layers. The first is a reparameterization of the problem. Under the standard unweighted objective, a domain’s sampling share controls both token exposure and its average contribution to the gradient. The authors fix the sampled-data mixture and instead multiply each domain loss by a domain-specific coefficient. This keeps the observed data stream unchanged while altering the relative pull each domain exerts on optimization. In controlled knowledge (K) versus mathematics (M) experiments, they show that K→M staging, M→K staging, direct mixing, and fixed loss reweighting land at different points in capability space even under matched 30B-token exposure. A suitable math coefficient can improve both MMLU and GSM8K simultaneously, even beyond the best values seen anywhere along the staged trajectories.

The second layer is the adaptive controller Lare, short for Loss-Adaptive Reweighting under fixed Exposure. Fixed coefficients work, but require expensive sweeps. Lare estimates useful domain weights online from running domain-loss statistics. After learning-rate warmup, it applies a normalized inverse-square-root rule to derive relative coefficients. Intuitively, this avoids letting high-loss domains dominate linearly while still increasing their optimization influence; the square-root form and normalization make the adjustment smoother. The normalization is important: the mixture-averaged coefficient remains one, so the method changes relative optimization scale across domains without globally rescaling the objective. This keeps the intervention focused on domain balance rather than effective learning-rate changes.

Relative to prior work, this is not another data-schedule search method and not a standard curriculum-learning variant. Its key contribution is to separate “what the model sees” from “how hard the model learns from it,” then show empirically that the second axis is independently powerful. It is also distinct from importance sampling or token-level weighting: the intervention is domain-level objective reweighting under fixed exposure.15:T5ad,The experimental design is one of the paper’s strengths. In the controlled K–M setting with matched 30B-token exposure, the authors compare K→M staging, M→K staging, several direct-mixture ratios, fixed loss reweighting, and Lare. Direct mixtures usually settle at an interior compromise between knowledge and math. In contrast, fixed reweighting—especially a 1:2 math coefficient under 7:1 K:M exposure—moves the model into a better region that exceeds both the knowledge peak and the math peak observed along the staged trajectories. Figure 1 is the key empirical result.

At larger scale, under 4× Chinchilla with K:M = 7:1, Lare improves over direct mixing by 0.39 on MMLU, 13.57 on GSM8K, and 8.40 on MATH. Extending training to 8× Chinchilla with additional math and code data yields gains of 0.83, 17.06, 9.00, 6.71, and 5.60 on MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MBPP, respectively, relative to direct mixing. This matters because it shows the effect is not confined to a toy two-domain setup and extends into code capability as well.

The paper also checks robustness across optimizers, sampled-data ratios, domain compositions, and training budgets. An important practical takeaway is that Lare may not beat an oracle fixed coefficient on every metric, but it reaches a competitive region of the trade-off in a single run, avoiding costly coefficient sweeps. For large-scale training, that is a meaningful systems-level advantage.16:T536,This one deserves a careful read. Start with the introduction and Figures 1–2, because the whole paper hinges on the distinction between exposure and optimization scale. A good reading order is: Figure 1, Section 2, the Lare formulation, Table 2, then the robustness appendices.17:T88e,方法核心很干净：forward-dense, backward-sparse。作者先利用一个经验事实：attention 训练里 backward 大约比 forward 更重，而且不同 query block 对梯度的贡献高度不均匀。于是 LazyFlash 保留标准 FlashAttention 前向，确保输出与 dense attention 完全一致；只在 backward 中按 block 粒度跳过“贡献很小”的 query blocks。

具体做法分三层。第一层是重要性度量。它不去显式估计完整 attention map 的重要性，也不做额外 teacher distillation，而是用每个 query block 的输出梯度范数来近似该 block 对参数梯度的贡献。这个选择的好处是信号直接来自当前训练步的反向传播，且与 FlashAttention 的 tile/block 结构天然对齐。

第二层是预算式稀疏化。作者不是预设固定 sparsity ratio，而是设定一个“允许丢弃的梯度质量比例”预算。先根据 block 级梯度质量排序，再决定哪些 block 可以被跳过。这样稀疏率会随训练阶段、样本、层而变化；当梯度分布更尖锐时，可以跳过更多 block；当梯度更平时，自动保守。这比固定 top-k 或固定阈值更稳，因为后者容易在不同 batch 和不同长度下失配。

第三层是无偏估计。若总是确定性地丢弃小梯度 block，会引入系统性偏差。LazyFlash 在预算内按与梯度贡献成比例的概率保留 block，并对保留项做重标定，从而让梯度估计保持无偏。这个设计很关键，因为它把方法从“启发式剪枝”推进到“受控随机近似梯度”。

实现上，作者把它做进 FlashAttention backward kernel，支持标准 dense 输入和 variable-length 输入。由于前向完全不变，训练出的模型仍是普通 dense attention 模型，推理时可直接用 vLLM 之类现成系统，不存在 train-inference mismatch。和 MoBA、SeerAttention、DSA 这类方法相比，LazyFlash 不需要前向稀疏选择器，也不需要 dense attention 蒸馏目标，因此训练侧节省是真实发生的；和从头预训练的原生 sparse attention 相比，它更适合已有 dense 模型的长上下文微调与继续训练。18:T7f9,The method is conceptually simple: forward-dense, backward-sparse attention. The forward pass is left unchanged and implemented with standard FlashAttention, so model outputs and serving behavior remain exactly those of a dense-attention model. Sparsity is introduced only in the backward kernel.

The first ingredient is block-level importance estimation. Instead of predicting sparse patterns from attention scores or distilling from a dense teacher, LazyFlash uses the norm of the output gradient for each query block as a proxy for that block’s contribution to parameter gradients. This is attractive because the signal is already available during backpropagation and aligns naturally with FlashAttention’s tiled computation.

The second ingredient is budget-based sparsification. Rather than fixing a sparsity ratio, the method sets a budget on how much gradient mass may be discarded. Blocks are ranked by gradient contribution, and the effective sparsity adapts to how concentrated the gradient distribution is at each step. This is more robust than fixed top-k or threshold rules, which can miscalibrate across batches, layers, or sequence lengths.

The third ingredient is unbiased estimation through importance sampling. Deterministically dropping low-contribution blocks would introduce bias. LazyFlash instead samples retained blocks with probability proportional to their gradient contribution and rescales them accordingly, yielding an unbiased gradient estimator. That is the key step that turns the method from heuristic pruning into controlled stochastic approximation.

Implementation-wise, the authors integrate this into a FlashAttention backward kernel and support both dense and variable-length inputs. Compared with methods such as SeerAttention or DSA, LazyFlash does not require computing dense attention targets for distillation, so the training-side savings are real. Compared with native sparse-attention pretraining methods, it is much easier to apply to existing dense models during long-context adaptation.19:T4d8,The main empirical results are speed and quality retention. On long-context text and long-form speech LLM settings, the paper reports up to 5.7x speedup for attention backward and up to 1.7x end-to-end training speedup. The gap between these two numbers is informative: even if attention backward is heavily accelerated, total training time still includes MLP compute, communication, optimizer overhead, and data pipeline costs.

On model quality, the paper claims that LazyFlash matches dense training closely while delivering those speedups. The most important evidence is not a single benchmark number but the stability-quality tradeoff under different gradient-mass budgets. The reported behavior suggests that gradient contribution across query blocks is strongly skewed, which is exactly the structural property the method exploits.

The most useful ablations are likely: fixed sparsity ratio versus gradient-mass budget, deterministic dropping versus importance-sampled unbiased estimation, gains as sequence length grows, and whether variable-length support preserves wall-clock benefits. For this paper, those ablations matter more than downstream benchmark breadth because the core contribution is a training-efficiency mechanism.1a:T45e,The analysis starts with an isotropic Gaussian noise baseline. In the fixed-dimensional low-SNR limit, applying the partial polar map to each stochastic gradient gives a conditional mean response that is, to first order, only a scalar multiple of the population gradient. The paper then studies associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. A key mechanism is nullspace preservation: if a task direction is absent from a mini-batch, Muon does not update that direction. For two tasks, the paper derives an exact balancing threshold; for rare tasks, B_bal scales as roughly (log 2) / p_min. For higher-rank task hierarchies, local perturbation estimates identify B p_j as the controlling scale. The label-noise analysis separates task counts B p_j from corruption counts B p_j rho_alpha, and an isotropic covariance closure predicts a Muon contraction coefficient scaling like sqrt(Bp), while SGD scales linearly with the local frequency p. The provided text does not expose the full ablation tables, so per-component gains should be read from the paper rather than inferred.1c:Tb07,方法上分成两半。第一半在已发布的大模型权重上做“精确重排”实验。作者先对 Huginn-3.5B、Ouro-1.4B、Ouro-2.6B 做 topology audit：给所有 normalization module 打桩，统计不同 loop count 下每个模块的调用次数，以此判断某个 norm 是在 loop 内部每步调用，还是只在 readout 路径上调用。审计结果显示，Ouro 的 model-level normalization 每个 loop step 都会调用，等价于存在 loop-boundary normalization；Huginn 则只在最终 readout 前调用。随后作者对 Ouro 做一个非常克制的改动：把这个 model-level norm 限制到最后一个 loop step 才执行。这样 readout path 保持 bit-identical，参数不变，而且在 r=1 时该改动严格是恒等映射，可作为实现正确性的检查。这个设计很重要，因为它把变化限制在“重新进入下一轮 loop 的状态”上，尽量排除了别的混杂因素。

机制分析上，作者没有停在 accuracy，而是同时跟踪四类信号：每个 loop step 的 state norm、readout entropy、logit margin、输入到预测的 mutual information。结果显示，去掉已训练模型中的 boundary norm 后，性能会在少数 loop step 内崩掉，但 state norm 只变化到最多 2.021 倍，远不到“尺度发散”能解释的程度；相反，readout entropy 会从 0.786 bits 飙到 12.470 bits，随后又回落，因为输出头开始把概率质量压到答案字母表之外，最后甚至塌成单一 token。作者进一步做了一个很有说服力的诊断：冻结 loop 主体后只重拟合 readout，损失只能恢复到约三分之一；若连最后一个 block layer 一起重拟合，则几乎能把损失全部找回。这说明问题不只是最后线性头的校准，而是 loop 末端表示与读出接口一起发生了错位。

论文还有一个方法学点：比较 loop depth 和 stack depth 时，若按绝对 K 比，会系统性偏向训练 loop count 更大的配置，因为它虽然看起来“更深”，但推理 compute 其实不等价。作者主张按 budget overshoot K/r0 比较，这同时也是等 compute 的比较方式。在这个口径下，looping 相对 stacking 的优势在 circuit 任务上检测不到，在 hops 任务上也会缩小而不是扩大。1d:Tb48,The study has two complementary halves. The first uses released large-model checkpoints and performs an exact topology intervention without retraining. The authors instrument every normalization module in Huginn-3.5B, Ouro-1.4B, and Ouro-2.6B, counting calls under different loop counts to determine whether a given normalization acts inside the loop or only on the readout path. This audit shows that Ouro applies its model-level normalization once per loop step, creating a loop-boundary normalization, while Huginn applies the corresponding module only once before readout.

They then modify Ouro in a tightly controlled way: the model-level normalization is restricted to the final loop step only. This keeps the readout path bit-identical, adds no parameters, and is exactly the identity when r=1, which serves as an implementation check. That intervention isolates the effect on the state that re-enters the next loop iteration while minimizing confounds.

The second half is causal: small looped models are trained from scratch with the topology fixed in advance, with and without boundary normalization. The models range from 19M parameters at 6 layers to 76M at 24 layers, across two task families, with 16 independent seeds per configuration on the normalization axis and 50 models overall. The unit of analysis is the training seed, and the paper uses exact rank tests and Cliff’s delta rather than relying on single runs.

Mechanistically, the paper goes beyond accuracy and tracks four signals: per-step state norm, readout entropy, logit margin, and input-to-prediction mutual information. This is where the argument becomes convincing. Removing boundary normalization from a model trained with it causes rapid collapse within a few loop steps, but state norm changes by at most 2.021x across the grid, which is far too small to support a residual-growth explanation. In contrast, readout entropy jumps from 0.786 to 12.470 bits on a one-bit task, then falls again as the head collapses onto tokens outside the answer alphabet. A further diagnostic strengthens the interpretation: refitting only the readout on top of a frozen damaged loop recovers only about one third of the loss, whereas refitting the last block layer together with the readout recovers essentially all of it. That localizes the failure to a mismatch at the loop-end representation/readout interface, not to generic numerical instability.

The paper also makes a methodological point about comparing loop depth to stack depth. Comparing at equal absolute K systematically favors the configuration with larger trained loop count r0, even though compute is not matched. The authors argue that equal budget overshoot K/r0 is the fair comparison because it also equalizes compute. Under that comparison, the apparent advantage of looping over stacking disappears on circuit tasks and shrinks on hops tasks.1e:T693,On released checkpoints, removing loop-boundary normalization from Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B causes severe failure near or before the trained loop budget. If reading time is limited, the best order is: Introduction → topology audit and exact intervention → from-scratch causal results → readout-refit diagnosis → depth-comparison methodology. A careful read should take about 60–90 minutes.20:Tb5f,技术方案可以分成四部分看。

第一部分是理论分析。作者先分析中间状态 s = αe_i + βz 的解码竞争关系。若用欧氏距离，候选 token 的得分会分解成一个随信号缩小而衰减的对齐项，以及一个与当前状态无关的静态范数项。问题就在这里：当 α 变小，即便 β=0、状态方向仍完全对准源 token，低范数 token 也可能因为静态范数优势而“反超”。这不是语义替换，而是度量退化。于是作者转到方向空间，用 cosine / directional ranking 来定义竞争，得到 pairwise crossing 的阈值条件：候选是否超过源 token，取决于有效噪声是否大于两者的语义分离。这个阈值理论把 token identity metric 从经验统计量还原成了大量 pairwise crossing 的聚合结果。

第二部分是 noising geometry。既然问题来自 norm decay，作者就不再沿普通连续高斯轨迹做 corruption，而是设计了 spherical noising。做法是把状态看成沿球面 geodesic 向一个 mask-biased endpoint 插值。这样可以尽量保持向量范数稳定，把竞争关系限制在方向空间里发生，避免欧氏几何下的伪竞争。这里的关键不是“球面”这个词本身，而是它服务于一个更明确的目标：让 corruption 过程和 token competition 的真实判据一致。

第三部分是时间调度，也就是 Semantic Retention Scheduling。Competition Threshold Theory 说明，大量 identity crossing 只会在接近高噪声端才发生。若仍用常规时间参数化，训练的大部分步数都浪费在身份几乎不变的区间，真正困难的身份转移区间反而预算很少。作者因此按 logarithmic rank decay 重新分配时间步，把更多 denoising budget 放到 identity 快速变化的区间。这不是简单的 loss-aware resampling，而是直接围绕 token rank / identity decay 设计 schedule。

第四部分是模型实例化，即 LLaCO。它基于预训练 backbone 适配到连续表示空间，包含 embedding directional adapter 和 timestep-conditioned modulation。前者负责把离散 token embedding 映射到适合方向竞争的连续空间，后者让 backbone 在不同噪声阶段采用不同调制。推理时，模型做 sequential blockwise denoising，并沿 spherical geodesic 逐步把连续语义轨迹翻译回离散 token。这里仍保留 blockwise 生成而不是一次性全序列并行，说明作者在生成质量与并行性之间做了折中：先把连续扩散的语义轨迹建稳，再逐步释放并行生成潜力。

和已有 continuous diffusion LM 相比，区别主要有三点：一是从经验 identity metric 转向解析阈值理论；二是从普通欧氏 corruption 转向方向一致的球面 noising；三是 schedule 不再围绕时间均匀性或损失均匀性，而是围绕语义身份保留来分配训练预算。21:T8b3,全文给出的核心实验结论是：LLaCO 在大规模实例化下显著优于此前连续扩散基线，并且已经接近同规模离散扩散模型。模型规模方面，作者明确实例化了一个 8B 模型，这是这篇工作的一个重要信号，因为很多连续扩散 LM 论文停留在中小规模验证，难以判断方法是否能撑到真正的 LLM 区间。

从实验结构看，最值得注意的不是单个 benchmark 分数，而是理论—指标—系统三层验证是否闭合。第一类实验验证理论：作者比较欧氏解码与 cosine / directional ranking 下的 overtaking 行为，显示欧氏度量会在低噪声甚至零噪声附近产生虚假反超，而方向空间的 crossing 更符合实际 token identity 衰减。第二类实验验证 schedule：作者测量预训练 embedding 上的 identity metric / rank decay，发现经验曲线与理论推导的 crossing aggregation 基本一致，并且常规时间参数化确实把大量身份变化压缩在尾部；重新分配后，训练步数更集中在高信息密度区间。第三类实验验证系统收益：LLaCO 在广泛 benchmark 上全面超过先前 continuous diffusion baselines，并与可比规模的 discrete diffusion 模型接近或相当。

从消融角度，最该关注的应是四组：directional decoding vs Euclidean、spherical noising vs standard noising、semantic retention scheduling vs conventional schedule、adapter/modulation 组件是否必要。论文主张较强，若这些消融成立，说明收益不是单点技巧，而是几何、调度、架构适配共同作用的结果。

摘要和引言没有给出完整表格数字，因此无法在不臆测的前提下逐项复述 benchmark 分数。但可以确定的硬信息有两点：一是模型规模为 8B；二是作者强调“comprehensively outperforms previous continuous diffusion baselines and rivals discrete diffusion models of comparable scale”。阅读正文时应重点核对：提升是否稳定覆盖语言建模、通用生成和采样效率相关指标；以及在相同采样步数、相同 backbone、相同 tokenizer 条件下，LLaCO 的增益有多少来自 schedule，多少来自 spherical noising。22:T978,The method has four tightly linked components.

First, the theory. For an intermediate state s = αe_i + βz, Euclidean decoding can be decomposed into an alignment term that shrinks with the signal and a static norm penalty that does not depend on the current state. This asymmetry creates a degeneracy: as α decreases, a lower-norm token may overtake the source even at zero noise. That is not semantic replacement; it is a metric artifact. The paper therefore switches to directional competition, effectively a cosine-based ranking view, and derives pairwise crossing thresholds. A candidate overtakes the source only when the effective directional noise exceeds their semantic separation. Existing token identity metrics are then reinterpreted as statistical aggregates of many such pairwise crossings.

Second, the noising geometry. Since the pathology comes from norm decay, the paper replaces standard continuous corruption with spherical noising. The trajectory is formulated as a geodesic interpolation toward a mask-biased endpoint, so vector norms are preserved more faithfully and competition happens in directional space rather than being distorted by Euclidean norm effects. This is an important design choice: the corruption process is made consistent with the competition criterion.

Third, the schedule. Competition Threshold Theory implies that in high dimensions, most meaningful identity transitions happen only at very high noise levels. A standard time parameterization therefore wastes much of training on regions where token identity barely changes, while under-allocating budget to the narrow transition zone. The proposed Semantic Retention Scheduling reallocates timesteps according to logarithmic rank decay, explicitly concentrating optimization where identity transitions occur.

Fourth, the model instantiation, LLaCO. A pretrained backbone is adapted to continuous representations using an embedding directional adapter and timestep-conditioned modulation. At inference time, generation proceeds through sequential blockwise denoising along spherical geodesics, translating continuous semantic trajectories back into discrete tokens. Compared with earlier continuous diffusion LMs, the novelty is not just a new schedule. It is the combination of a directional theory of token competition, a norm-preserving corruption path, and a schedule aligned to semantic retention rather than raw time.23:T869,The main empirical message is that LLaCO scales beyond toy settings and performs substantially better than prior continuous diffusion baselines, while becoming competitive with discrete diffusion models at similar scale. The instantiated model is 8B, which is itself notable because many continuous diffusion LM papers stop at much smaller scales.

The most useful way to read the experiments is as a three-level validation stack. First, theory validation: the paper compares Euclidean decoding with directional ranking and shows that Euclidean distance produces premature overtaking, including near-zero-noise artifacts, whereas directional competition better matches actual identity decay. Second, schedule validation: empirical identity metrics and rank decay measured on pretrained embeddings track the theoretical crossing behavior, and standard trajectories indeed compress most identity transitions near the noisy endpoint. Third, system validation: once spherical noising and semantic-retention scheduling are built into the model, LLaCO consistently beats earlier continuous diffusion baselines across a broad benchmark suite and approaches discrete diffusion performance.

The most important ablations are likely the following: Euclidean vs directional decoding, standard vs spherical noising, conventional vs semantic-retention scheduling, and the contribution of the directional adapter plus timestep modulation. If these ablations are strong, the gains are not a fragile artifact of one engineering trick but the result of aligning geometry, scheduling, and model adaptation.

For a serious assessment of whether this paradigm is worth following, the theory sections need a full read.25:T6ea,NESTOR introduces nested sparsity. The model first routes each token to a small subset of attention columns, and then, within each selected column, applies standard MoE-style expert routing in the feed-forward path. Concretely, each block contains C columns, and a column router selects Kc active columns per token. Each column has its own attention parameters and computes causal attention only over the subset of tokens routed into that column. This creates two kinds of attention-side sparsity at once: parameter sparsity, because a token only uses a subset of attention parameters, and map sparsity, because attention is computed only within the routed token subset. Inside each column, each layer then has E experts, of which Ke are selected by an expert router, giving the usual MoE sparsity on the MLP side. The effective computation path for a token is therefore hierarchical: column selection times expert selection. This differs from standard sparse-attention methods, which mainly reduce the attention map while keeping parameters shared, and from mixture-of-attention-head approaches, which often route attention more locally and independently per layer. NESTOR’s design is more structured: the attention subnetwork itself is conditionally selected, and that selection naturally nests with MoE routing. The paper emphasizes three distinct but coupled sparsity axes: attention-weight sparsity, attention-map sparsity, and expert sparsity. That framing is useful because it suggests the gains come not only from fewer FLOPs but from better allocation of model capacity. In continual pretraining, this structured routing may also help absorb new domains or longer contexts through specialized subpaths rather than by overwriting a large shared parameter core.26:T624,The experiments have two main parts. First is compute-efficient pretraining. The authors compare dense transformers, standard MoE transformers, and NESTOR across scales from roughly 100M to 1B active parameters. The headline result is that NESTOR achieves 1.13–1.29× better compute efficiency than MoE and 3.1–4.1× better than dense transformers, and the advantage does not appear to vanish as scale increases. The important signal here is the downward shift in the loss-vs-compute curve, not a single benchmark number. Second is continual pretraining. The models are adapted to several specialized domains, and the comparison tracks both gains on the new domains and retention on the original pretraining distribution. NESTOR reportedly gains about as much as MoE on each new domain while forgetting less, and it does so with fewer training FLOPs per token on the continual data. The long-context extension setup increases context length from 4k to as high as 64k, and NESTOR maintains its advantage over MoE when models receive equal amounts of continual-pretraining tokens. That control matters because long-context improvements are often confounded by extra adaptation compute. The abstract does not expose all absolute losses, downstream metrics, load-balancing numbers, or ablation details, but the full paper likely includes comparisons among partial variants that activate only one or two sparsity axes. The two deeper questions worth carrying forward are whether this routing pattern scales cleanly in distributed training, and how much of the gain comes from capacity allocation versus an inductive bias toward document-local structure.28:T733,The method has three main components. First, elastic expert dimensions. Each MoE expert is turned into a Matryoshka-style nested FFN: instead of training multiple independent experts at different widths, the same parameter tensors support several inner dimensions. During training, a target width D_k is sampled, and only the first D_k hidden channels are used in the expert’s SwiGLU computation. At inference, this allows deterministic slicing of the same checkpoint into smaller expert variants, reducing both parameter residency and activation cost. The paper also notes an important stability issue: shrinking the inner dimension changes the scale of the down-projected activations, which can disturb residual addition and RMSNorm statistics, so a compensation or rescaling mechanism is introduced. Second, adaptive sigmoid routing. Rather than top-k softmax routing, the router produces independent sigmoid gates for experts and compares them against a learned, task-conditioned threshold. This lets each token activate a variable number of experts. Harder tokens can use more experts, easier tokens fewer. Compared with top-k, this relaxes fixed-FLOP control but enables finer-grained compute allocation. Third, a dual-consistency objective. Because training sees multiple capacity views—different widths and different routing patterns—the model is regularized with an in-place self-distillation loss that aligns predictive distributions across these nested structures. The key point is that no external teacher and no post-training adaptation are required; the consistency signal is built into the original training run. In addition, the architecture includes a Direction-Aware Shared Expert computed in parallel, intended to capture translation-direction-specific shared patterns and reduce over-reliance on sparse experts alone.29:T54a,The experiments cover PhoMT for English–Vietnamese, WMT14 for English–German, multilingual OPUS-16, and a multi-domain German–English benchmark. This gives the method a reasonable spread across bilingual, multilingual, and multi-domain heterogeneity. At a high level, the full-capacity EDWARD-NMT improves over Transformer Big and is competitive with recent lightweight MoE baselines. The more interesting result is on extracted subnetworks: the smallest variant, EDWARD-NMT-S, is not separately trained but sliced from the same checkpoint, yet still outperforms a dense Transformer Base. That is the main empirical support for the “train once, deploy anywhere” claim. If the paper includes active-expert histograms, quality-versus-memory curves across width slices, and ablations on consistency regularization, those are the parts to focus on.2a:T5b0,Key insight: selection outputs a discrete set of indices; top-k is non-differentiable, and backward only needs the k selected scores. Therefore, you can (i) avoid materializing the full score table and (ii) avoid rerunning selection during recomputation.

HyScale implements this via:
1) HyTopK: an on-the-fly, exact top-k operator that maintains top-k while scoring, eliminating the full score table. It is deterministic and CP-compatible. It uses a threshold-filtering idea with an “optimistic threshold” and a rare/cheap recovery path to keep exactness without slowing down.
2) Selection replay: record forward-pass selection results and, during activation recomputation, replay only the k selected entries needed for the indexer loss—rather than recomputing selection over all prior tokens. This moves recomputation granularity below the operator level to “only what the indexer loss needs.”
3) End-to-end integration on Megatron-LM: once selection is faster, CP communication and sparse kernels become visible bottlenecks. HyScale overlaps CP collectives for sparse attention behind selection (decoupled CP overlap) and introduces locality-aware sparse kernels that process adjacent queries together to reuse loads/updates for shared entries.

A notable design choice is insisting on exact top-k (vs sampling/approximation) for determinism and training stability, while using replay to avoid paying the recomputation cost of exact selection.2b:T43f,Deep-read plan (1.5–2 hours):

At 704×1280 resolution, spatial overlap processes each token 2.03 times on average, so roughly half of per-token computation is duplicated. Larger tiles cause about an 11.9 dB drop, while reducing overlap to 16 pixels costs about 0.34 dB. Intervention results show that MiniMax-H3 needs 4 of 36 layers kept per tile, MAGI-1 needs 3 of 24, and ViTok-v2 needs none. Short self-distillation can remove the remaining per-tile layers for MiniMax-H3.2d:T8ee,方法核心是一个由 Taylor 一阶展开驱动的误差分解。作者把最终输出记为 O，把第 l 层注意力输出记为 A^(l)，把模型视为 O = G(A^(0), ..., A^(L-1))。当对某层 KV cache 做压缩时，会引入该层局部扰动 ΔA^(l)。在小扰动假设下，最终输出偏差可以用一阶多元 Taylor 展开近似，从而得到两类因素：

1）Local Approximation Error，记作 E_l：表示第 l 层压缩本身造成的信息损失。
2）Layer-wise Structural Sensitivity，记作 S_l：表示该层扰动经由后续网络被放大的程度，通常可由梯度范数或相关敏感度指标近似。

有了这个分解，系统设计就对应两条线。

第一条线是降低 E_l。作者认为现有 merging 方法的主要问题是忽略了 RoPE。RoPE 会对 query/key 施加位置相关旋转，导致 token 在旋转后的空间里不再适合直接按原始相似性做合并。于是他们把 token aggregation 放到 Pre-RoPE 的“安全区”，即在位置旋转之前进行聚合。为了避免简单合并导致注意力质量守恒被破坏，方法还引入 attention-conserving logit bias，在物理合并 token 时尽量保持原有注意力质量分布。这里的直觉是：不是只保留 token 数量，而是尽量保留被这些 token 支撑的注意力质量。

第二条线是管理 S_l。作者不满足于知道哪些层敏感，而是把 memory management 写成动态资源调度问题：在总内存固定、希望达到近似 O(1) 占用的前提下，按层分配不同 KV budget。具体做法是利用 offline gradient priors 估计各层敏感度，然后把更多预算留给高敏感层，从低敏感层更激进地回收内存。这样做的含义是，压缩不再是所有层一刀切，而是层感知的非均匀分配。

整体上，这是一个 hybrid framework：Pre-RoPE aggregation 负责减少局部误差，sensitivity-aware budget allocation 负责抑制误差放大。它是 training-free、model-agnostic 的，不需要重新训练底座模型。和已有方法相比，区别主要有三点：一是给了一个明确的误差分析，而不是纯经验规则；二是把合并位置前移到 RoPE 前；三是预算分配按层敏感度动态调度，而不是固定比例压缩。2e:T8f8,The method starts from a first-order Taylor analysis. Let the final model output be O and the attention output at layer l be A^(l). The model is abstracted as O = G(A^(0), ..., A^(L-1)). Compressing the KV cache at layer l introduces a local perturbation ΔA^(l). Under a small-perturbation assumption, the final output deviation can be approximated by a first-order multivariate Taylor expansion, yielding two factors:

1) Local Approximation Error E_l: the information loss caused directly by compression at layer l.
2) Layer-wise Structural Sensitivity S_l: how strongly perturbations at layer l are amplified by the rest of the network, estimated through gradient-based signals or related sensitivity measures.

This decomposition drives two design components.

The first component minimizes E_l. The authors argue that many existing merging methods ignore the effect of RoPE. Since RoPE applies position-dependent rotations to queries and keys, the post-RoPE space is no longer a clean space for similarity-based token merging. Their solution is to perform token aggregation in a Pre-RoPE 'safe zone,' before positional rotation. To avoid losing attention mass during physical token consolidation, they introduce an attention-conserving logit bias so that the merged representation better preserves the original attention distribution.

The second component manages S_l. Instead of using a uniform compression ratio across layers, the paper formulates memory management as a dynamic resource scheduling problem under a fixed memory budget. Offline gradient priors are used to estimate layer sensitivity, and more KV budget is assigned to high-sensitivity layers while low-sensitivity layers are compressed more aggressively. In other words, compression becomes layer-aware rather than uniform.

Overall, the framework is hybrid: Pre-RoPE aggregation reduces local approximation error, and sensitivity-aware budget allocation controls downstream error amplification. It is training-free and model-agnostic, so it does not require retraining the base model. Compared with prior work, the differences are clear: an explicit error decomposition instead of pure heuristics, merging before RoPE rather than after it, and non-uniform layer-wise budget scheduling instead of fixed-ratio compression.2f:T5e1,The headline result is explicit in the paper: on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Video-MemComp improves overall accuracy from 62.3% to 64.1% while limiting the average KV cache to 6,000 tokens per layer, reducing KV-cache memory by more than 90%. This is the paper’s 'less is more' result: removing redundant or harmful history can improve accuracy rather than merely preserving it.

The evaluation is conducted on benchmarks including MLVU, Video-MME, and EgoSchema, and across multiple MLLM architectures. The experiments support four main claims. First, under very low memory budgets, the method can match or even surpass the full-cache baseline. Second, the gains come from both parts of the design: Pre-RoPE aggregation lowers local approximation error, while layer-wise budget allocation reduces error accumulation. Third, layer sensitivity is highly non-uniform, so uniform compression across layers is suboptimal. Fourth, RoPE-aware handling matters; merging after RoPE performs worse.

The most informative ablations are likely the following: with and without Taylor-guided sensitivity, with and without the Pre-RoPE safe zone, with and without the attention-conserving logit bias, fixed versus dynamic budget allocation, and accuracy-memory curves under different cache budgets. Even without reproducing every table entry, the main message is clear: the method does not rely on extra training to recover performance; it improves memory efficiency by making compression itself more principled at inference time.30:T654,Read this paper by first understanding the analytical motivation, then the engineering choices.

Start with the introduction and the beginning of the method section. The first-order Taylor expansion is not there as a formal theorem; it is there to produce an actionable surrogate objective that separates local compression loss from layer sensitivity. Once that framing is clear, the rest of the method becomes easy to follow.

Then read the Pre-RoPE aggregation section carefully. Two questions matter: why the post-RoPE space is a poor place for token merging, and how the attention-conserving logit bias compensates for changes in attention mass after merging. This is the most distinctive engineering idea in the paper.

After that, read the layer-wise budget allocation section. The key issue is not the optimizer details, but how offline gradient priors are estimated, how budgets are assigned, whether calibration data is needed, and whether sensitivity is stable across samples. This part is highly transferable to long-context text LMs.

In the experiments, prioritize the main table, the memory-accuracy tradeoff curves, and the ablation tables. If the goal is only to decide whether the paper is worth following up, 25-35 minutes is enough. If the goal is to adapt the idea to text LMs or unified multimodal LMs, spend another 20 minutes on the appendix for implementation details, complexity analysis, and sensitivity visualizations. The most interesting open question is whether the sensitivity prior can be updated online, or even reflected in pretraining so that representations become easier to compress.31:T448,The paper asks a narrow but important question: do halting heads in looped language models actually convert low predicted iteration counts into real compute savings at inference time? The answer is often no. The mismatch comes from two places. First, the standard training objective is misaligned with the execution rule. With the common mixture loss, the halting head is trained through a mixture of hidden states from all iterations, while inference stops on one discrete iteration chosen by a thresholded cumulative halting rule. So the model can report low expected halting steps yet still run almost to the cap under the actual stopping rule. Second, batching changes the compute story again: even if some tokens halt early, the batch waits for the deepest token, so average token depth is not the same as realized batched compute. The paper is therefore not just about adaptive depth in the abstract. It is about where the training objective, stopping rule, and execution system fail to line up, how large that gap is, and how halting should be evaluated if one wants honest compute claims.32:T40a,This matters for pretraining-oriented model design because looped LMs and recurrent-depth LMs are often motivated by the promise of adaptive compute without extra parameters. The paper shows that this promise can be overstated if one reports only expected halting steps. More broadly, it is a clean case study of train-test mismatch in adaptive computation: a probabilistic training signal does not automatically translate into useful discrete decisions at inference. That lesson extends beyond looped LMs to early-exit transformers, pondering methods, and other conditional-compute schemes. It also contributes a practical reporting standard: expected steps, realized steps under a stated exit rule, and batched execution depth should all be reported. Finally, the paper proposes a pre-head diagnostic that estimates how much a halting mechanism could help before one spends effort training it. The contribution is not a new architecture. It is a careful correction to how this line of work should be trained, compared, and measured.33:T7c9,The technical contribution is mainly analytical and experimental. First, the authors dissect the standard ACT-style mixture loss. In that setup, the language-model loss is computed from a hidden state formed by mixing representations from all iterations according to halting probabilities. This is convenient for optimization, but it gives the model access to a representation that is never available at inference, where the token exits at one concrete iteration. The paper quantifies this mismatch by replacing the mixture readout with the actual single-step state and showing a substantial degradation. Second, the authors test a PonderNet-style per-step loss, where every iteration is scored and the losses are weighted by the head’s own halting probabilities. This is much closer to the real execution path because the model is trained on all possible exit points. But the paper shows that this alone is still insufficient. Without a strong prior favoring early stopping, the learned distribution remains too conservative and realized savings stay weak. Section 6.2 is especially useful: the issue is not simply whether one supervises every step, but that the head also controls the weighting over steps, which encourages a self-consistent allocation of probability mass toward later iterations. Third, the evaluation protocol is upgraded from token-level expectations to actual execution. The paper separately measures expected halting steps, realized steps under the thresholded exit rule, and the number of iterations a batched pass really executes. This separation is central because it isolates three different objects that are often conflated. The paper also discusses a deployment detail that turns out to matter: in single-sequence generation, halted tokens have no fresh KV states for skipped iterations, yet later tokens may still attend to them there. Reusing halted tokens’ KV states is therefore treated as part of the method definition, not a minor implementation choice.34:T8cb,The study trains looped models from 140M to 1.3B parameters, on two text corpora, mostly with three seeds, using a cap of 8 iterations. The main findings are consistent and fairly sharp. (1) With mixture-loss training, heads often predict fewer than 4 out of 8 iterations on average, but under the standard 90% cumulative-probability exit rule the realized depth remains close to the full 8. In other words, the headline expected depth reduction does not translate into actual compute reduction. (2) Forcing earlier stopping hurts quality quickly. Once the saving exceeds roughly one iteration, a same-size sampled-depth baseline—trained without a halting head, simply with randomly chosen iteration counts—outperforms the halting model at the same compute budget. That is a strong baseline result because it shows the halting mechanism can lose to a simpler training recipe on the quality-compute frontier. (3) The train-test mismatch is large in language-model terms: replacing the mixture state with the actual single-step state costs about 0.2 BPB, while the gap between the smallest and largest models in the paper is about 0.24 BPB. So the mismatch is not a minor artifact; it is comparable to a substantial scaling gain. (4) Per-step loss only works when paired with a strong early-stop prior. Without that prior, the objective is more faithful to inference but still does not produce useful realized savings. (5) Batching removes most of the remaining advantage. On whole-text evaluation, the per-step model can beat the sampled-depth baseline at matched average depth; in generation with batches of 32 sequences, the actual batch depth rises well above the average token depth and most of the advantage disappears. (6) The same phenomenon is observed for Ouro, a released looped LM with a trained halting head. (7) In single-sequence generation, some benefit survives if halted tokens’ KV states are reused across skipped iterations, but even then the model does not beat a specialist trained to run at a fixed depth of about three iterations. The experimental arc is well structured: invalidate the common metric, identify the loss-level cause, add the systems-level effect, and compare against simpler baselines under matched compute.35:T427,For a quick but useful read, start with the Introduction and Figures 1–2. The paper only makes sense once the distinction among expected halting steps, realized steps, and batched execution depth is clear. Then go to Section 5.2, which contains the central negative result: mixture-loss heads appear to halt early in expectation but barely save compute under their own stopping rule. After that, read Section 6, especially 6.2, for the explanation of why per-step training still needs a strong prior. That section is where the paper moves from observation to mechanism. Finally, read Section 7 for the deployment-facing analysis of batching and KV reuse. If time is limited to 20–30 minutes, the Introduction, Section 5.2, Section 7, and the reporting recommendations are enough to capture the main message. The authors use OpenCode as a fixed agent scaffold and implement five compaction strategies as drop-in replacements for the default compaction logic. They then evaluate four frontier models on three realistic long-horizon benchmarks. The study is organized around four questions. First, threshold sensitivity: they sweep the token threshold that triggers compaction, from 160K to 380K, and measure downstream task performance. Second, strategy sensitivity: they compare default self-summarization against alternatives such as using a smaller model to summarize, removing reasoning blocks, and writing the pre-compaction context to disk as a near-lossless external memory. Third, constraint retention: on tasks with explicit anti-cheating rules, they inspect how many constraints survive the first and subsequent compactions. Fourth, benchmark bias: they compare benchmark trajectories with real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat to see which kinds of information are disproportionately lost. The contribution is less about a new algorithm and more about turning compaction from an implementation detail into a measurable experimental factor.37:T64d,The evaluation covers PaperBench, ProgramBench, and PostTrainBench, using Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, with two runs per task/configuration. Several results stand out. First, for the 1M-context models, changing the compaction threshold from 160K to 380K does not materially affect task performance. GPT-5.3-Codex, with a smaller 400K context window, degrades more clearly at lower thresholds on PaperBench and shows a weaker similar trend on PostTrainBench. Second, no compaction strategy consistently beats default self-summarization, including the near-lossless strategy that writes the full pre-compaction context to disk. This suggests that preserving information externally is not enough; the model must also know when and how to retrieve and reconstruct state from it. Third, more aggressive strategies can hurt some models substantially: removing reasoning blocks or summarizing with a smaller model can cost up to about 20 points on PaperBench for certain models, while leaving others nearly unchanged. That model-specific interaction is one of the most useful findings. Fourth, on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops roughly one of the task’s three anti-cheating rules on average, and the loss compounds with repeated compactions. Fifth, in real SWE-chat sessions, compaction drops instructions about how the agent should work, and what it should avoid doing, about six times more often than it drops specifications of what to build. That result explains why benchmark outcomes can look reassuring while real interactive use remains fragile.38:T43c,GS-MoE compresses experts along two axes. The first axis is groupwise subspace sharing. Experts are partitioned into groups, and each group has its own shared projection matrices. Each expert keeps expert-specific projections inside the group subspace, so the method does not force every expert in a layer to use one common basis. The second axis is intermediate-width compression. Each expert keeps a different number of hidden neurons, selected using ridge-leverage scores. The up projections are fit through a group-level surrogate and expert input statistics. For the down projections, the reconstruction objective has a closed-form solution before width compression, and Nyström reconstruction maps retained hidden activations into the shared coordinates. Capacity allocation is also calibration-driven: per-expert reconstruction-error reductions guide grouping, while a gradient-free layer-importance score based on normalized, gate-weighted expert output magnitudes guides budget allocation across layers. Eigenvalue-based scores and parameter costs further guide group ranks.39:T51b,BiLoCo approximates each weight matrix as W ≈ R + \sum_{i=1}^{r} \alpha_i (v_i u_i^T), where R is the NVFP4-quantized residual and u_i, v_i are binary sign vectors in {±1} (bit-packed), plus per-component scalar coefficients \alpha_i. Inference then replaces multiply-accumulate in the correction with sign-controlled add/subtract accumulations, which maps naturally to CUDA cores.

A key algorithmic issue is that the optimal sign-vector decomposition is not given by SVD. The paper fits rank-one components greedily (following prior sign-decomposition work): initialize signs randomly, alternate updates of u and v for a few steps, compute the best scale \alpha for that component, subtract it from the residual, and repeat. After all components are fitted, it re-solves all \alpha jointly via least squares to account for overlap/correlation among components, then quantizes the remaining residual to NVFP4.

On the systems side, the implementation is a fused single kernel on Blackwell: the main NVFP4 GEMM runs on Tensor Cores; the binary correction is computed on CUDA cores within the same launch; the correction is added in the GEMM epilogue. The design is explicitly motivated by decode-shape behavior where Tensor Cores are memory-stalled and CUDA cores can be overlapped rather than contended.3a:T4ca,NgramRL uses the policy’s own recent rollouts as a free, self-updating drafter.
- Empirical observation: GRPO revisits the same prompts across steps/epochs and the policy changes incrementally, so completions for a given prompt are highly repetitive over time. The paper quantifies this locality (48–96% coverage of a later rollout by a prior one; recurring spans of 7–23 tokens).
- Drafter: a per-prompt n-gram table built from a bounded window of recent rollouts. Given the current context, it proposes continuations via lookup (model-free), and the target policy verifies them using standard speculative decoding accept/reject, preserving the exact output distribution.
- Runtime co-design: naive CPU-host lookup can serialize with GPU decoding, causing large GPU idle due to host round trips. NgramRL introduces an asynchronous multipath prefetcher: during GPU verification, the CPU prefetches drafts for likely next-step verification outcomes (indexed by outcome states such as (j, b)). An adaptive fan-out policy (a causal budget allocator) decides which branches to prefetch so most steps avoid post-verification host synchronization; uncovered branches fall back to synchronous lookup without changing semantics.3b:T502,Two components.
1) LEMS (Layer-wise Error Modeling Search): instead of allocating ranks using uncalibrated local sensitivity metrics, LEMS builds a layerwise surrogate that mixes (a) local sensitivity/importance, (b) global layer importance, and (c) an explicit bias term to account for error accumulation/propagation through depth. With this surrogate, the rank allocation under a global parameter/rank budget is formulated as an ILP, enabling principled global search rather than greedy allocation.
2) KFAC-SVD: starts from Fisher-weighted SVD where the loss increase is approximated by a second-order expansion with the Hessian approximated by the Fisher matrix, then uses a Kronecker-factored approximation F ≈ A ⊗ G to obtain a Frobenius objective in whitened coordinates (G^{1/2} W A^{1/2}). The key change is how A and G are estimated: token-wise statistics rather than sequence-wise aggregation. The motivation is that sequence-level aggregation yields low effective rank under limited samples (rank collapse), while token-wise accumulation increases statistical support and stabilizes the Kronecker factors, improving the truncated SVD fidelity. The final compressed layer is implemented as two consecutive dense linear layers (C(Bx)), keeping inference kernels simple.3c:T7f9,The work has two components: the benchmark and the harness. On the data side, LongVideo / 4DMemoryBench includes both multi-evidence questions within a single long video and cross-episode, cross-season, and full-series questions. The task mix covers visual, textual, temporal, and spatiotemporal reasoning. The important design choice is not just longer videos, but evidence dispersed across multiple temporal scales and scene transitions, forcing episodic recall and multi-hop temporal binding.

On the system side, the paper introduces the 4DMemory Harness / 4DMemory Agent. The design principle is task-independent storage plus goal-directed recall. This is meant to decouple task duration from the native context window of the underlying model. Unlike methods that depend on internal vision-token pipelines or model-specific post-training, the harness is presented as a model-flexible inference framework with a plug-in style interface.

From the full text, the harness integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and model-specific retrieval/routing components. The core idea is not to train one monolithic model, but to decompose long-horizon reasoning into stages: memory construction, coarse-to-fine retrieval, specialist evidence acquisition when needed, and final reasoning by the foundation model. The paper repeatedly emphasizes that long-horizon performance should be studied as a composition problem across memory, retrieval, tool use, and reasoning, not just as a context-length problem.

Relative to prior work, the differences are clear. It evaluates systems rather than only models. It avoids tight coupling to a single model’s internal token pipeline. And it explicitly treats memory construction, retrieval, skill selection, and reasoning as separate bottlenecks that can fail independently.3d:T695,The key confirmed scale numbers are: about 900 hours of video, 1,000+ videos plus two multi-season TV series, and 5,000+ manually reviewed QA pairs. The main findings are straightforward. Starting from a real paper, the authors extract a research context and reconstruct an original experiment proposal as a self-contained item. They then design a validity-relevant flaw and apply a minimal edit to produce a tampered proposal. After that, they perform faithfulness repair and self-containment repair so that the original remains faithful to the source paper and the tampered version is worse only along the intended methodological dimension, not because of missing context or poor wording. Finally, items go through admission filtering for quality and difficulty control. Evaluation is pairwise, but importantly each pair is tested in both presentation orders. The paper reports both per-order accuracy and both-orders accuracy; the latter only gives credit if the model picks the original in both orders, making it a direct measure of order sensitivity. This is a stronger test than a single comparison because many models produce locally coherent rationales yet flip their judgment when the order changes. The paper makes clear that the hard part of full-duplex modeling is not only real-time overlap between listening and speaking, but long-horizon stability under continual self-conditioning. That is different from standard long-context text LMs because token production is much denser and the model’s own acoustic-linguistic outputs are constantly reintroduced into the stream. For researchers working on speech token LMs, streaming multimodal models, or conversational audio systems, the paper offers two useful lessons. First is the benchmark, FD-LHB, with two complementary tracks. FD-LHB-CANDOR replays long human conversations from CANDOR, enabling controlled comparison across models for up to 60 minutes. Second is the diagnosis of failure. The authors evaluate five recent full-duplex models spanning two history-management strategies: growing-context and sliding-window. Both fail, but in different ways. For sliding-window models, the paper identifies two mechanisms. Initialization-Anchor Eviction refers to the eventual removal of the very first KV entry computed under empty-cache conditions; once that anchor is evicted, silence and gibberish become much more likely. The authors interpret this as evidence of a mismatch between empty-cache training and continual inference. Self-Reinforcing Repetition is the second mechanism: recently produced words become more likely to be produced again, creating a positive feedback loop that can collapse into repetition. Third, the paper proposes two training-free interventions. Initialization-Anchor Pinning keeps the first KV entry permanently in cache while the rest of the window slides. Duplex Repetition Penalty discourages recently used words without broadly suppressing the model’s tendency to speak. The two methods can be combined and still run in real time.43:T5ca,The benchmark construction itself is substantial. The fault model has three dimensions. The first is failure mode: timing failures versus content failures. Timing failures include delays, hangs, and missing responses; content failures include wrong values, malformed payloads, and schema/type violations. The second is persistence: permanent, transient, and intermittent faults. This is an important design choice because agent recovery behavior depends heavily on whether an error is persistent or bursty. The third is the injection schedule, which specifies when faults occur and is seedable for reproducibility.

A strong point is that the fault mix is calibrated rather than hand-crafted. The authors mine 57,240 issue and pull-request threads from 1,774 open-source MCP repositories and estimate the observed distribution over failure mode × persistence. The injected scenarios are therefore tied to reported ecosystem incidents instead of synthetic worst-case examples.

The evaluation is a full-factorial design: three agent stacks, two backbone sizes, three fault conditions, 25 tasks, and three seeds, for 1,350 experimental cells. The stacks include a custom multi-round plan-and-execute system, OpenAI Agents SDK, and another mainstream framework. This setup is meant to separate model scale effects from framework-level error-handling effects such as retries, exception propagation, and output validation.4c:T448,Three findings matter most. Second, differences across agent stacks are substantial, suggesting that framework-level handling of tool failures matters more than backbone scale in this setting.
